title: The Afternoon Brief: Japan Quake Toll Rises to 18 as Europe Fires Persist
dek: Southern Japan's earthquake toll rose to at least 18 people as rescue crews kept working two collapse sites, while European wildfires kept 330,000 people displaced and Washington closed out several long-running threads.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: The Japan earthquake death toll has risen to at least 18 as of the most recent reporting, up from an unconfirmed count reported Tuesday, while rescue operations continue at collapsed structures including the Aeon Mall in Kashima.
bottom_line: Southern Japan's earthquake death toll rose to at least 18 people, according to the desk's most recent reporting, up from Tuesday's unconfirmed count, as rescue crews continued working two collapsed sites including the Aeon Mall in Kashima. European wildfires kept roughly 330,000 people displaced across France and Spain, with the Gironde fire described by French officials as stabilized but not extinguished. Washington closed several long-running threads Tuesday: the Senate confirmed Jay Clayton as director of national intelligence, advanced a Russia and Iran sanctions bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, and held Graham's funeral at Washington National Cathedral, while a federal judge blocked Minnesota's prediction market ban and a Georgia court sentenced Colt Gray to life without parole. Coming checkpoints include Wednesday's Senate hearing on COVID origins, continued rescue and casualty confirmation in Kumamoto, and containment progress against the Gironde fire as heat returns to the region.
body: The throughline today is aftermath: a natural disaster in Japan whose toll is still climbing, wildfires in Europe still displacing people by the hundreds of thousands, and a string of long-running Washington and legal stories reaching their resolution points on the same day.

A 7.1-magnitude earthquake (the U.S. Geological Survey measured it at 6.8) struck southern Japan's Kyushu island on July 28, centered near Kumamoto. As the desk's earliest reporting on the quake noted, police in Kashima said there were "a lot of deaths" at the Aeon Mall shopping complex but could not immediately confirm an exact toll; nine people were unaccounted for at the mall and five had already been rescued from the same site. The picture has since hardened: the desk's most recent reporting puts the toll at at least 18 dead and at least 62 injured, including six in serious condition, per the Kumamoto prefectural government, with rescue crews still working two major collapse sites and an unclear number of people still missing. Tsunami alerts issued after the quake, forecasting waves of about one yard, were lifted, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged residents to stay away from coastlines and stay alert for aftershocks.

In Europe, wildfires in southwestern France and Spain have displaced roughly 330,000 people. French authorities ordered nearly 4,000 additional evacuations from Atlantic coast tourist sites around Lacanau. The Gironde fire west of Bordeaux, burning an area four times the size of Paris, has forced 220,000 evacuations on its own and is described by authorities as "stabilized, not fixed." Interior Minister Laurent Núñez called the operation likely the largest civilian evacuation in France outside wartime, and Gironde prefect Sophie Brocas said Tuesday, "we're not out of the woods." Spain has declared its first-ever national wildfire emergency as temperatures approach 40 degrees Celsius.

Several Washington and courtroom threads also closed today. The Senate confirmed Jay Clayton as director of national intelligence 51-47, ending the interim tenure of acting DNI Bill Pulte. A federal judge blocked Minnesota's first-in-the-nation prediction market ban, ruling federal commodity law preempts the state statute, with six other states pursuing similar bans now facing the same legal question. A Georgia judge sentenced Colt Gray, 16, to life without parole for the 2024 Apalachee High School shooting that killed four people, after Gray pleaded guilty to all 55 counts. Sen. Rand Paul released more than 1,000 pages of Fauci's journal entries ahead of Wednesday's Senate hearing on COVID origins. The Senate also advanced a bipartisan Russia and Iran sanctions bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, whose funeral drew President Trump, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu, and Ukrainian President Zelenskyy to Washington National Cathedral. Separately, the U.S. delegation walked out of a UN Security Council meeting after France compared the American vote against extending the UN human rights commissioner's term to votes cast by North Korea and Russia. In Peru, Keiko Fujimori was sworn in as president after a runoff decided by fewer than 50,000 votes. And in Seattle, a 15-year-old was ordered held in juvenile detention over a shooting at the Bite of Seattle festival that killed three people, as police continue searching for a possible third suspect.

The reporting does not offer a single driver tying these stories together beyond timing; each is following its own institutional calendar, from Japan's disaster response to the Senate's confirmation and legislative schedule to Georgia's criminal courts.

Desk boards were not available for this edition, so today's figures rely solely on the desk's published stories, with the most recent reporting on the Japan earthquake toll superseding Tuesday's unconfirmed count.

In the coming days, watch Wednesday's Senate hearing on COVID origins featuring the Fauci diary material, further passage and White House action on the Graham sanctions bill, an expected appeal in the Minnesota prediction market case, the search for a third suspect in the Seattle shooting, and continued rescue operations and casualty confirmations in Kumamoto as well as containment progress against the Gironde fire in France.
